title: Huntington Bank Launches Gemini-Powered AI Platform for Small Businesses
excerpt: . Huntington Bank has launched The 1866 Studio, a Google Gemini-powered platform using AI agents to help entrepreneurs start, finance and manage small businesses. SHARE. Huntington National Bank has launched an artificial intelligence platform designed to help small-business owners handle tasks ranging from starting a company to preparing for loans and creating marketing campaigns. Contents. AI Agents Will Help Owners Run Daily Business Tasks Loan Readiness Becomes Part of AI Banking Huntington Wants Platform to Cover Entire Business Lifecycle Google Cloud Pushes AI Deeper Into Banking. Called The 1866 Studio, the platform was built with Google Cloud’s Gemini technology and uses AI agents to help entrepreneurs manage financial, operational and business tasks from a single interface. The platform takes its name from the year Huntington was founded. Early-access registration opened on October 19 and is available even to entrepreneurs who are not Huntington Bank customers. FCRF’s Chief AI Officer Certification Returns on November 14 to Prepare Future AI Leaders. AI Agents Will Help Owners Run Daily Business Tasks. The 1866 Studio is designed to go beyond a traditional banking app. Huntington says the system will use agentic AI workflows that can help business owners move from receiving information to actually completing tasks. An AI agent differs from a normal chatbot because it can perform a sequence of actions rather than simply answer a question. For example, an entrepreneur starting a new company could use the platform to work through business registration, licensing and operational requirements. The system can then produce a customised plan outlining the steps required to launch the business. Another set of AI tools will help companies generate marketing material, digital advertisements and social-media campaigns using Google’s Gemini models. The platform is also designed to retain relevant business context across tasks, meaning owners should not need to repeatedly provide the same information as they move between different activities. Huntington says users will remain in control of the actions carried out by the system. Loan Readiness Becomes Part of AI Banking. One of the more significant features involves business financing. The platform will include an AI-powered loan-readiness tool designed to help business owners understand whether they are prepared to apply for financing. The system can identify potential weaknesses, explain what lenders normally expect and recommend steps that may strengthen a future application. That could include improving financial records, addressing gaps in business planning or preparing supporting documentation. The feature does not mean the AI itself approves loans. Instead, it is intended to help entrepreneurs better understand what may affect their chances of obtaining finance. For banks, that creates a new way to interact with potential borrowers before they formally apply for credit. It also moves AI deeper into the relationship between financial institutions and small businesses. Huntington Wants Platform to Cover Entire Business Lifecycle. Huntington says The 1866 Studio will eventually support entrepreneurs from the earliest stages of creating a company through growth, succession or a potential sale. The initial version focuses on business launch support, marketing and financing preparation. More AI agents are expected to be introduced over the next year. Huntington President Brant Standridge said the bank wants the platform to become part of the everyday operating environment for small businesses. The strategy could also help the bank attract customers who initially sign up only for the AI tools. Huntington currently operates more than 1,400 branches across 21 US states and has around $284 billion in assets. The bank is already a major small-business lender. excerpt: World Launches AI Identity Tools for Banks. In Short. Sam Altman-backed World has launched three identity products for banks, aiming to fight deepfake fraud and help AI agents prove identities online. Kahekashan. Created On: 19 Oct 2026 2:39 PM IST Comment. Share :. X. World Launches AI Identity Tools for Banks. Font size. Select Hans India Now. FOLLOW ON G o o g l e News. Sam Altman-backed World has introduced a new identity verification suite designed for banks and financial companies as artificial intelligence makes online impersonation and fraud increasingly difficult to detect. The company shared its offering through World co-founder Alex Blania at the Money20/20 conference on Sunday. This suite includes three products, each targeting a part of digital identity. One helps people show who they really are. Another checks who is in a video call to make sure it’s the person. The third lets AI agents use identity info to do tasks for users. These tools work together to make digital identity easier and safer. The move comes as financial institutions face a growing challenge from AI-generated faces, cloned voices and automated systems. These technologies can make it increasingly difficult to determine whether a person accessing an account or taking part in a business interaction is genuine. World says its products can provide an additional identity layer for customer accounts, employee processes and AI-powered services. The first product, the World ID app, allows users to access and share digital proofs of information about themselves. World ID for Zoom is designed to help people confirm that they are interacting with a real person rather than a deepfake during video calls. The feature is now generally available following a limited beta that began in April. The third offering, World ID for Agents, also called AgentKit, takes the concept further by allowing users to delegate their identity proofs to AI agents. Those agents can then present credentials to third-party platforms while completing tasks on behalf of their users. World has named Open Exchange, Bain Capital, VanEck Funds and Outtake as design partners exploring how the technology could be used in financial services. However, the company has not disclosed pricing or identified a bank that is currently using the system. World claims that more than 18 million people have a Proof of Human credential. It also cited a Deloitte estimate that losses linked to AI-driven fraud in the US could increase from $12. 3 billion in 2023 to $40 billion by 2027. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang calls for stronger AI security. The launch comes as the technology industry debates how businesses should deal with the cybersecurity risks created by increasingly capable AI systems. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has rejected the idea that companies should simply accept cyberattacks as AI advances. Speaking to Fortune earlier this week, Huang said, “I'm willing to accept no incidents of cybersecurity. We should not accept any of them. ” He added that companies should do everything possible to prevent such incidents. His comments differ from recent remarks by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to Vanity Fair, in which Altman warned about an approaching wave of cybersecurity challenges, including threats involving competing open-source AI models. Huang argued that stronger monitoring and containment could have prevented such incidents and has advocated keeping AI agents inside secure environments with restricted access. The debate highlights a key challenge for the AI industry: giving agents enough access to independently complete tasks while preventing them from exposing sensitive information or creating new security vulnerabilities. The launch addresses concerns about AI-generated faces, synthetic voices and automated systems that can make it difficult to determine who is accessing financial accounts or participating in online transactions. World says the technology could provide an additional verification layer across banking services, employee workflows and AI-powered applications. The first product, the World ID app, allows users to access and share digital proofs of personal information. The second, World ID for Zoom, is designed to help video-call participants verify that they are interacting with real people rather than deepfakes. The feature is now generally available following a limited beta launched in April. The third product, World ID for Agents, also called AgentKit, enables users to delegate identity credentials to AI agents. These agents can present verified credentials to third-party platforms while performing authorised tasks. Are Banks Using the Technology?. World has identified OpenExchange, Bain Capital, VanEck Funds and Outtake as design partners exploring potential applications in financial services. The launch comes amid wider concerns about autonomous AI systems accessing sensitive information and operating across digital platforms. World’s identity verification system addresses one aspect of these risks by attempting to establish whether an online interaction involves a verified person or an authorised AI agent. title: The blueprint for financial leadership: Building a self-driving WAN for the AI era
summary: AI is transforming finance, but legacy networks hinder progress. Learn how AI-native WANs enable fraud detection, trading, payments and innovation with better security.
excerpt: An article from. Sponsored. The blueprint for financial leadership: Building a self-driving WAN for the AI era. Published Oct. 19, 2026. By Joe Fuchs Global Industry GTM Lead and Cyril Doussau, Routing Infrastructure PSM Leader. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. Sponsored content. By Hewlett Packard Enterprise. SPONSORED CONTENT BY. Financial services AI is moving from the back office to the front lines, with 32% to 39% of work across capital markets, insurance, and banking poised for full automation 1. However, as institutions race to deploy generative AI and autonomous agents, they are colliding with a physical wall: their legacy network infrastructure. These new workloads fundamentally reshape WAN requirements, driving massive traffic across distributed locations where strict latency and predictability are critical. Traditional networks simply were not designed to handle data moving at this scale between AI clusters, clouds, branches, and the edge. Consider an ordinary Tuesday morning at a modern, global financial institution. In Singapore, a fraud model flags an unusual wire and routes it for human review, but the alert takes eleven seconds to reach the analyst's queue from the AI cluster in the primary data center. By the time she opens the case, the payment has cleared. In London, an underwriter waits on a model that ingests satellite and aerial imagery for commercial property renewal; the file times out twice before the risk score returns, and the broker calls back before she can quote. In New York, a quant team's overnight backtest finishes ahead of schedule, then sits idle for forty minutes while the results copy across a saturated link to the research environment. All these problems demonstrate that an AI-powered process can only be as fast as its slowest component, and only as secure as its least secure component. Financial organizations are not just consuming cloud-based AI; 68% of enterprises favor training and customizing their own private AI models 2. Rapid advancement in GPU and other accelerator technology has created a new bottleneck in the process: the ability to safely route data in and results out of AI servers and clusters. As AI factories scale, they are generating data volumes that push traditional WAN architectures to their absolute breaking point. In HPE’s recent keystone study, “AI’s Impact on Wide Area Networking,” in partnership with Omdia, we found that large enterprises expect their AI traffic loads to grow 5x in the next 3 years. AI training and inferencing traffic is multiplying at 140%+ CAGR, and 96% of enterprise AI adopters train or customize their own models 2. Nokia Bell Labs recently predicted WAN traffic could grow up to 700% by 2034 3. What the Network Looks Like from the Desk, the Branch, and the Claims File. Network constraints rarely announce themselves as network constraints. They surface as a missed quote, a stalled claim, an alert that arrives after the money has moved, or a model that cannot be explained to a regulator. The practitioners who feel this first are almost never in the networking organization:. Traders, market data teams, and quants: On the trading floor, the network is the strategy. Market-data multicast and cross-venue routing depend on highly deterministic, low-latency delivery; a jittered feed is indistinguishable from a bad price. Conversely, research teams face idle GPU clusters waiting on data movement—turning an intraday insight into a next-day one. Idle accelerators are the most expensive equipment in the building. Payments and treasury operations: Real-time payment rails, ISO 20022, and 24x7 settlement have eliminated the overnight batch window that once let operations absorb network delays. Today, continuous sanctions screening and intraday cash positioning mean every network hop between the core system and the operator's console subtracts time from an already narrow release-or-hold decision. title: The next AI decision financial institutions must get right
summary: As AI moves into production, infrastructure strategy becomes a competitive differentiator.
excerpt: An article from. Sponsored. The next AI decision financial institutions must get right. Published Oct. 19, 2026. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. Sponsored content. By Schneider Electric. SPONSORED CONTENT BY. Artificial intelligence has quickly moved from innovation labs into core business operations. Banks are using AI to strengthen fraud detection. Trading organizations are deploying AI to analyze market activity in real time. Insurance providers are accelerating underwriting, claims processing, and risk assessment. Across financial services, institutions are investing aggressively in AI to improve efficiency, deliver better customer experiences, and uncover competitive advantages. Yet as many organizations move beyond pilots and begin scaling AI into production, a fundamental question is emerging:. Where should AI actually run?. The answer carries significant implications for performance, security, regulatory compliance, operating costs, and long-term business agility. For years, the cloud was viewed as the logical destination for advanced analytics and emerging technologies. However, AI is changing the equation. Large-scale AI workloads create new power, cooling, networking, and governance requirements that force organizations to reassess traditional infrastructure strategies. At the same time, financial institutions face growing pressure to control sensitive data, meet regulatory obligations, and support mission-critical operations without introducing additional risk. Many financial services organizations are discovering that infrastructure decisions have become business decisions. For applications such as fraud detection, transaction monitoring, algorithmic trading, and customer interactions, milliseconds matter. AI systems often need to process information close to where data is generated to deliver real-time insights and responses. Moving everything to centralized environments can create challenges around latency, costs, and operational control. Data sovereignty adds another layer of complexity. Financial institutions manage some of the most sensitive information in the world. Regulatory expectations around data privacy, governance, and auditability continue to evolve. As AI becomes more deeply embedded in financial operations, organizations must evaluate how deployment models affect security, compliance, and control over business-critical data. The result is that many organizations are moving toward a more deliberate infrastructure strategy. Rather than asking whether AI should run in the cloud or on-premises, leading institutions are evaluating a broader range of options, including cloud services, colocation providers, modernized data centers, and hybrid deployment models. Each approach carries different advantages depending on business priorities, workload requirements, and risk tolerance. According to Schneider Electric's research, factors such as data sovereignty, latency, time-to-market, scalability, staffing expertise, cash flow preferences, and total cost of ownership should all be considered before determining where AI workloads should reside. For many organizations, AI success will not be determined solely by algorithms or models. It will depend on whether infrastructure can support AI's growing demands while preserving resiliency, security, and operational control. The organizations that succeed will be those that align infrastructure decisions with business outcomes, creating an environment where AI can scale efficiently without compromising governance, performance, or customer trust. title: Wie KI den Kundenservice im Banking verändert
excerpt: Beeindruckende KI-Demos gibt es viele – produktive Anwendungen im Banking deutlich weniger. Woran liegt das eigentlich? Ein Blick hinter die Kulissen eines KI-Assistenten für den Kundenservice zeigt, was zwischen Prototyp und Go-Live wirklich zählt. Künstliche Intelligenz gilt als Schlüsseltechnologie für die Zukunft des Bankings. Dennoch scheitern viele Initiativen daran, den Sprung vom Experiment in den produktiven Betrieb zu meistern. Am Beispiel eines KI-Assistenten für den Kundenservice, der aktuell auf den Go- Live vorbereitet wird, zeigt dieser Beitrag, welche Voraussetzungen erfüllt sein müssen, damit generative KI echten Mehrwert für Kunden, Mitarbeiter und Unternehmen schafft. Partner des Bank Blogs. KI im Banking: Zwischen Erwartungen und Realität. Kaum eine Technologie hat in den vergangenen Jahren für so viel Aufmerksamkeit gesorgt wie Künstliche Intelligenz. Die rasanten Fortschritte der generativen KI haben die Erwartungen von Unternehmen, Kunden und Investoren gleichermaßen befeuert. Viele Banken haben daher Pilotprojekte gestartet und strategische KI-Initiativen aufgesetzt. Gleichzeitig zeigt sich ein wiederkehrendes Muster: Die Zahl der erfolgreichen produktiven Anwendungen bleibt hinter den Erwartungen zurück. Während die Technologie beeindruckende Fähigkeiten demonstriert, fällt es vielen Instituten schwer, daraus nachhaltig messbaren Geschäftsnutzen zu generieren. Die Gründe sind vielfältig: fehlende Business Cases, regulatorische Anforderungen, unzureichende Datenqualität und häufig eine unterschätzte organisatorische Verankerung und Nutzerakzeptanz. Die zentrale Frage lautet daher nicht mehr, ob KI eingesetzt werden sollte, sondern wie der Schritt von der technischen Möglichkeit zur nachhaltigen Wertschöpfung gelingt. Ein Beispiel dafür liefert unser KI-gestützter Assistent für den Kundenservice. Kunden erwarten sofortige und verlässliche Antworten. Im Kundenservice sind die Erwartungen an Geschwindigkeit und Qualität besonders hoch: Kunden möchten ihre Anliegen möglichst schnell lösen und erwarten zunehmend dieselbe Verfügbarkeit und Reaktionsgeschwindigkeit, die sie von digitalen Plattformen anderer Branchen kennen. Gleichzeitig steigen Umfang und Komplexität der verfügbaren Informationen kontinuierlich. Produktinformationen, Preis- und Leistungsverzeichnisse, regulatorische Vorgaben oder Serviceprozesse müssen aktuell gehalten und konsistent beantwortet werden. Für Serviceorganisationen entsteht dadurch ein Spannungsfeld zwischen hoher Servicequalität und operativer Effizienz. Traditionelle Chatbots konnten diese Herausforderung bislang nur teilweise lösen. Viele Systeme basieren auf vordefinierten Dialogbäumen und geraten schnell an ihre Grenzen, sobald Kunden individuelle Fragen stellen oder Themen miteinander kombinieren. Große Sprachmodelle eröffnen hier neue Möglichkeiten. Die Herausforderung besteht darin, ihr Potenzial mit den hohen Anforderungen an Sicherheit, Nachvollziehbarkeit und Verlässlichkeit im Banking zu verbinden. Ein Assistent, der die Frage versteht – nicht nur das Schlagwort. Vor diesem Hintergrund entstand unser KI-gestützter Assistent für den Kundenservice. Er befindet sich aktuell in der finalen Vorbereitung auf den Go-Live. Das Ziel war nicht ein weiterer klassischer Chatbot, sondern ein intelligenter Assistent, der Kundenanfragen in natürlicher Sprache versteht und relevante Antworten auf Basis bestehender Wissensquellen bereitstellt. Der entscheidende Unterschied: Informationen werden nicht lediglich anhand von Schlagworten gesucht. Das System interpretiert die Bedeutung einer Anfrage und kann dadurch auch komplexere Fragestellungen nachvollziehen. Fragt ein Kunde beispielsweise nach den Bedingungen eines Wertpapiersparplans oder den Voraussetzungen für bestimmte Handelsmöglichkeiten, erhält er künftig nicht nur einen Verweis auf eine Dokumentenseite. title: CEOs of major banks grilled at Assembly audit over AI cyberattacks
excerpt: FSS governor vows thorough probe into data breaches. The heads of five major commercial banks faced scrutiny at a National Assembly audit Monday over a series of recent artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyberattacks, with lawmakers raising concerns about cybersecurity and internal controls. KB Kookmin Bank CEO Lee Hwan-ju, Shinhan Bank CEO Jung Sang-hyuk, Hana Bank CEO Lee Ho-seoung, Woori Bank CEO Jung Jin-wan and NH NongHyup Bank CEO Kang Tae-young were summoned as witnesses to the parliamentary audit of the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS). It was the first time since October 2022 that the heads of all five lenders had been called to testify at the same audit. "I sincerely apologize to our customers and the public for the concern caused by a security incident at a financial institution built on trust," KB Kookmin Bank CEO Lee Hwan-ju said. "We will make every effort to prevent a recurrence by securing sufficient budgets and personnel and strengthening our security systems against AI-powered cyberattacks. ". "I deeply apologize for the incident," Shinhan Bank CEO Jung Sang-hyuk said in response to a question from Rep. Kim Jae-sub of the main opposition People Power Party about the data breaches. Hana Bank CEO Lee Ho-seoung said the lender would "increase its cybersecurity budget and workforce and adopt AI-based security systems to prevent similar incidents. ". Lee said the bank would compensate customers in full for any losses resulting from the incident, although no customer losses had been confirmed so far. "We face around 200 hacking attempts a day, and our employees will do their utmost to prevent any damage," Woori Bank CEO Jung Jin-wan said, adding that the bank considered itself fortunate to have escaped harm in the recent wave of attacks. The bank chiefs were summoned after a wave of suspected AI-linked cyberattacks hit financial institutions in recent weeks. As of Oct. 14, 16 financial firms, including banks, savings banks and insurers, had reported cybersecurity incidents that exposed about 100,000 personal records, according to financial authorities. Among the affected lenders, Shinhan Bank reported a data breach involving about 25,000 people, while KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank reported leaks affecting 119 and 89 customers, respectively. Woori Bank and NH NongHyup Bank have not reported customer data breaches linked to the recent incidents. The incidents have raised concerns about vulnerabilities in banks' security systems. Rather than directly targeting core banking networks, the attacks involved abnormal access to internal support systems, prompting suspicions that AI agents may have been used to automate the process. Financial regulators and law enforcement authorities have been conducting investigations to identify perpetrators. FSS Gov. Lee Chan-jin pledged to address the vulnerabilities exposed by the breaches by investigating thoroughly. "The recent security breaches have caused great concern among the public. We will swiftly address security vulnerabilities through a thorough investigation," the governor said during the audit. He added that the watchdog will encourage financial institutions to use AI to strengthen their defenses against AI-powered attacks. "We will consult with the Financial Services Commission to review various measures aimed at encouraging financial institutions to increase their investment in security and personnel," he said. How city leaders can build a smarter, more integrated response to climate-related events
excerpt: . Smart cities are often data rich but insight poor. An effective city-wide response to the increasing number of climate-related events, such as flooding and heat islands, demands better insight built on integrated data and operating models. At a glance:. Urban resilience rests on data-interoperability – the ability to connect and use data – across multiple agencies to establish a shared operating picture. Bringing all the data together under the auspices of a single city support center can speed up a unified response to climate events. AI-powered digital twins help cities to anticipate how a climate risk event may evolve and to identify areas of immediate impact. AI agents can assist operators at every step of the incident management response – veracity check, correlation of events, dynamic action plan creation and execution, and continuous monitoring and intelligence generation. The right analytics capabilities enable city leaders to predict climate events and make faster, evidence-based risk mitigation decisions. Torrential rain has caused a river to burst its banks, flooding tunnels and blocking transport routes. Who responds? The water authority pumping out water and managing the clean-up? The transport department rerouting traffic and diverting trains? The first responders? Or all together in a coordinated manner?. Similarly, the summer heatwave has created an urban heat island. Extreme high temperatures can have an impact on public health, transport systems, workforce productivity, and more. Who takes the lead? The health authority, transport operators, or municipal authorities? And who communicates with the citizens?. In both the above climate-impact scenarios, we typically see a multi-agency response. However, while there may be well-established procedures and processes in play, each agency often focuses on its own operational responsibilities. This means that there is limited coordination across the wider system and very little data transparency between all the players. With climate-related events on the rise, this operational and data disconnect is giving city leaders and policy makers a big headache. In the following article we offer an alternative, more connected route to managing climate risk events utilizing a centralized support center, integrated data, and AI. What is the impact of a siloed response to climate events?. For public sector leaders getting to grips with the impact of our changing environment, a siloed response can be both costly and, crucially, life threatening. It can lead to delayed interventions, inefficient resource deployment, duplication of effort, counterproductive actions, and reduced community resilience. Maintenance spending also rises in response to (potentially preventable) damage caused, further adding to the pressure on already over-stretched local government budgets. Climate risk events can evolve rapidly. Ideally, the fragmented information they generate should be rapidly coordinated across public safety, transport, utilities, health, municipal operations, and community services. Instead, however, the disconnected data sources and resulting limited situational awareness mean that operators often struggle to get a clear picture of the bigger story unfolding before them. They are also often dealing with manual coordination processes and pressure to make critical decisions with constrained resources. An AI-native approach moves the area of impact beyond fragmented sensors, cameras, citizen reports, and agency systems to establish a correlated, unified shared operating picture.
